questions.question: A 10-second event-time window covers [0, 10). The current watermark is t=16s and allowed lateness is 5 seconds. What should happen to a newly arriving event with event time t=9s in the lesson model?
options: It enters the first window result because processing time is irrelevant
It produces a late update because all late records are retained forever
It is too late because the watermark has moved past the window end plus allowed lateness
It starts a new window at t=16s
questions.explanation: The window ends at t=10s and is retained through the configured lateness boundary. At watermark t=16s, that retained boundary has passed, so the record needs an explicit too-late policy such as a side output.

questions.question: Why is event time usually preferred for a result that must reproduce the same business grouping after replay?
options: Event time is derived from the record and does not change when backlog or recovery changes processing time
Event time guarantees that records always arrive in order
Event time removes the need for watermarks
Event time makes every sink transactional
questions.explanation: Processing time depends on when the runtime handles a record and can shift after failure or backlog. A stable event timestamp preserves the intended business-time grouping.

questions.question: What is the most important distinction between watermark delay and allowed lateness?
options: They are two names for the same setting
Watermark delay postpones the first firing, while allowed lateness retains fired-window state for later updates
Allowed lateness changes operator parallelism
Watermark delay controls checkpoint storage
questions.explanation: The watermark determines event-time progress and first firing. Allowed lateness controls how long state remains after that firing and whether accepted late records can update the result.

questions.question: A job fails while checkpoint 7 is still in flight. Which restore point can Flink use?
options: Checkpoint 7 because it had started
The latest checkpoint that completed successfully before the failure
The next scheduled checkpoint
Any TaskManager's newest local state, even if other tasks disagree
questions.explanation: A coordinated checkpoint becomes a recovery point only after its required participants and storage actions complete. An incomplete snapshot cannot define one consistent job state.

questions.question: Why can an arbitrary HTTP payment call still execute twice even when Flink managed state uses exactly-once checkpointing?
options: HTTP calls are always made by the JobManager
Replay can execute user code again, and the external call is outside checkpoint coordination unless it has a transaction or idempotency contract
Exactly-once applies only to processing-time windows
Checkpointing disables source position recovery
questions.explanation: Flink coordinates managed state and supported source and sink boundaries. An external effect needs a checkpoint-aware connector or an application-level idempotency key and reconciliation strategy.

questions.question: What does keyBy make possible for managed keyed state?
options: Every subtask can update the same key concurrently
Records with the same key and their state are assigned to one logical key-group owner
One hot key is automatically split across every subtask
State no longer needs checkpoints
questions.explanation: Keyed partitioning colocates a key's updates with its state. Key groups let Flink redistribute ownership during rescaling, but one hot key remains one key and can still create skew.

questions.question: Which operational action best starts a Flink backpressure investigation?
options: Increase parallelism for every operator immediately
Disable checkpointing to remove all coordination
Locate the affected subtasks and compare busy, backpressured, idle, checkpoint, skew, and sink signals along that path
Replace event time with processing time
questions.explanation: Backpressure propagates from a constrained path. Subtask-level graph and metric evidence identifies whether the cause is CPU, skew, state, checkpoint alignment, network, or an external sink.
